title: Testing: test design, doubles, boundaries and the test pyramid
seriesDescription: Test design, mocks versus fakes, integration and contract tests. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Test-case design with boundaries and equivalence classes, test doubles, the test pyramid, contract tests, flaky-test causes, coverage and mutation scores, and short SQL and shell checks.
source: Martin Fowler (TestDouble, TestPyramid, Mocks Aren't Stubs); Google Testing Blog (Flaky Tests); Pact documentation (consumer-driven contracts); Myers, The Art of Software Testing (boundary value analysis); Pitest and mutation testing literature

questions.prompt: A form accepts ages from 18 to 65 inclusive. How many test inputs does classic two-value boundary value analysis use (one just outside and one on each boundary)?
questions.explanation: The values are 17, 18, 65 and 66: the two boundaries plus the neighbour just outside each. Add a typical value in the middle for the equivalence class if you want.

questions.prompt: The same form accepts ages from 18 to 65 inclusive and rejects everything else. Into how many equivalence classes does that split the integer inputs?
questions.explanation: Below 18 (invalid), 18 to 65 (valid) and above 65 (invalid). One representative value from each class is enough to cover it, and boundaries then add the sharp edges.

questions.prompt: A function `parseDate("dd/mm/yyyy")` returns a calendar date. Which inputs are worthwhile edge cases? Select all that apply.

options.why: Correct: a special calendar case that must be accepted.
Correct: a well-formed string that must be rejected.

options.text: An empty string and a missing value.
options.why: Correct: absent input is a classic failure mode.
It adds no new behaviour beyond the typical case already covered.

questions.explanation: Edge cases come from boundaries, invalid input, empty values and special calendars.

questions.prompt: Match each test double with its role.

right.text: Passed around to fill a parameter but never actually used
Returns canned answers to calls made during the test
A real or stub object that also records how it was called
Pre-programmed with expectations that it verifies
A working but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory database
A copy of production data loaded for performance tests

questions.explanation: The terms follow Gerard Meszaros and Martin Fowler. In everyday speech "mock" is often used for all of them.

questions.prompt: Complete the structure of a well-formed test.
questions.text: A test follows {1}, {2}, {3}: set up the inputs and state, run the code under test, then check the outcome.
questions.explanation: Keep one Act per test and assert on behaviour. Names such as given/when/then describe the same shape.

questions.prompt: Which mix of automated tests does the test pyramid recommend?

options.text: Mostly end-to-end browser tests with a small handful of unit tests.
options.why: That is the inverted pyramid: slow, brittle and hard to diagnose.

options.text: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a few end-to-end tests.
options.why: Correct: cheap, fast, precise tests at the base.

options.text: Equal numbers of every kind of test, so each layer is covered the same.
options.why: The cost and speed of the layers differ widely.

options.text: Only manual testing before release, since automation is too expensive.
options.why: Manual-only testing does not scale or catch regressions fast.

questions.explanation: The shape follows cost and feedback speed. Modern variations (testing trophy, honeycomb) put more weight on integration tests for service architectures.

questions.text: A consumer-driven {1} test (for example Pact) checks that a provider still honours what consumers rely on, without a full {2} environment, while tests of a pure function with plain inputs are {3} tests.
questions.explanation: Contract tests catch breaking API changes early, which is what makes independent deployment of services safe.

questions.prompt: A test passes alone but fails in the full suite, and also fails near midnight. What is the most reliable cure for the time-related failure?

options.text: Add a two second sleep before the assertion so the clock ticks over.
options.why: Sleeping makes the test slower and still depends on the real clock.

options.text: Retry the test up to five times in the CI configuration.
options.why: Retries hide the flake instead of fixing its cause.

options.text: Inject a clock (or freeze time) so the test controls "now".
options.why: Correct: removes the dependency on the real wall clock.

options.text: Run the whole suite only during the daytime hours.
options.why: Scheduling around the problem leaves the defect in place.

questions.explanation: Flaky causes: shared state, ordering, time, randomness, concurrency and real network calls. Isolate each by injecting or seeding it.

questions.prompt: True or false: tests that share a mutable database without cleaning up after themselves can pass when run alone but fail in the full suite.

options.why: Correct: leftover rows from one test change the starting state of another.
Test order and leftover data are a common source of order-dependent failures.

questions.explanation: Give each test its own data (transaction rollback, unique ids or a fresh container) so tests can run in any order and in parallel.

questions.prompt: A mutation-testing tool creates 40 mutants of the code. The test suite fails (kills) 34 of them. What is the mutation score as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number?
questions.explanation: 34 / 40 = 0.85, so 85 percent. The 6 surviving mutants point at behaviour that no test pins down, which line coverage alone cannot reveal.

questions.prompt: A feature must work on 3 browsers, 2 operating systems and 4 locales. How many configurations does the full cross product contain?
questions.explanation: 3 x 2 x 4 = 24. Pairwise (all-pairs) testing covers every pair of values with far fewer cases, which is why it is used when the product grows quickly.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A test suite can reach 100% line coverage and still miss defects.
questions.reason: Coverage measures which lines were executed, not whether the tests assert anything useful about the results.

whys.a: Correct: A line can run without any assertion checking its output, so coverage alone proves little.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Use coverage to find untested code, not as proof of quality. Mutation scores and review of assertions complement it.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Replacing every collaborator with a mock in a test proves that the real components work together.
questions.reason: A mock only verifies interaction with a stand-in, not the behaviour of the real dependency.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: the integration is never exercised. R is true and is exactly the gap.

questions.explanation: Keep unit tests isolated with doubles, and add a small number of integration tests that use the real database, queue or HTTP client.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A consumer-driven contract test lets teams detect breaking API changes without running every service together.
questions.reason: Unit tests of pure functions run in milliseconds.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but the speed of unit tests has nothing to do with how contract tests detect incompatibilities.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: The contract is a recorded set of consumer expectations that the provider verifies in its own pipeline.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Any random generator used in a test should be seeded with a fixed value.
questions.reason: A seeded generator produces the same sequence on every run, so a failure can be reproduced.

whys.a: Correct: Reproducibility is the point: a failing run can be repeated exactly.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: For property-based testing, print the seed on failure so the failing case can be replayed.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Tests should not depend on the order in which they run.
questions.reason: Test runners always execute tests in exactly the order in which they were written.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because order dependence causes flaky suites. R is false: many runners shuffle or parallelise tests.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Run the suite in random order and in parallel in CI to expose hidden coupling between tests.

questions.prompt: In test-driven development, what do you do right after writing a test and watching it fail (red)?

options.text: Rewrite the test until it passes without touching any production code.
options.why: Weakening the test defeats its purpose.

options.text: Delete the failing test and write a larger integration test instead.
options.why: Skipping the small step abandons the cycle.

options.text: Write the simplest code that makes the test pass (green).
options.why: Correct: minimal code to go from red to green.

options.text: Refactor the whole module before the first test has ever passed.
options.why: Refactoring comes after green, with the test as a safety net.

questions.explanation: Red, green, refactor. The failing test first proves the test can fail, so a later pass is meaningful.

questions.prompt: Write a SQL query that returns each `email` from the `users` table that appears more than once, together with its count. Use it as a data-quality test: it should return zero rows when the data is clean.

checks.label: filters groups with more than one row

questions.model: SELECT email, count(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING count(*) > 1;
questions.explanation: The same shape tests a uniqueness assumption before adding a `UNIQUE` constraint. Other valid forms use a window function or a self-join.

questions.prompt: Write a curl command for a smoke test that calls `https://staging.example.com/health` silently, fails the command on any HTTP error status, and gives up after 5 seconds.
questions.explanation: A non-zero exit code makes a CI step fail. Combine short flags as `-fsS -m 5` if you want errors still printed (`-S`). Smoke tests check that the deployment is alive, not that every feature works.
